entries.title: Medusa
entries.imageAlt: Sepia-toned ink portrait of Medusa with coiling snakes woven through her hair.
entries.teaser: Perseus takes her head. He does not take her voice.
story: The last thing Medusa heard before the blade was her youngest snake hissing, 'Left.' She turned left. Perseus was already on the right. Bronze flashed without a face behind it, the curved sword passed cold through her throat, and the floor struck her cheek with surprising gentleness. For one breath she smelled salt, iron, and the wild fennel her sister Stheno had crushed for supper. Then Perseus lifted her by the hair and put her in the dark.

She woke inside a goatskin sack while he was flying. Wind punched the leather. Winged sandals beat an uneven rhythm outside. Medusa had no lungs, yet she drew breath; no body, yet every snake on her head was alive and furious. One of them found a seam and bit Perseus through the tunic. He shouted, dropped twenty feet, recovered, and swore by Zeus. 'Wrong god,' Medusa said from the sack. His silence was so complete she could hear the sea below them. 'Athena sent you,' she added. It was not a question.

Behind them, Stheno and Euryale screamed across the island. They were immortal and could afford a long grief. Medusa, the only mortal Gorgon, had always been the sister who counted hours, mended nets, remembered when the figs would turn. Now her sisters hunted a man hidden beneath Hades' cap while two newborn creatures rose from the blood at her severed neck: Pegasus striking sparks from the rocks, Chrysaor lifting a golden blade to the dawn. Medusa felt both sons leave the world through a door she could not follow. 'Fly faster,' she told Perseus. 'My sisters have your scent.'

He flew faster. The sack swung against his hip. Through the snakes, Medusa tasted the old bronze of Athena's shield and remembered the goddess arriving at her temple after Poseidon had gone. Athena had carried the same stillness then: not mercy, not rage, but the hard attention of someone deciding where to place a weapon. Medusa remembered her own hair falling across her shoulders. She remembered the first hiss close to her ear. She had screamed. Then one snake had whispered her name, and she had stopped.

At the coast of Ethiopia, Perseus saw a woman chained to a black rock and forgot his hurry. Andromeda stood above a boiling sea while her mother's court watched from the cliffs in ceremonial silence. The monster below was all jaw, barnacled spine, and ancient appetite. 'Put me down,' Medusa said. Perseus gripped the sack. 'I know what happens when I do.' 'So does the monster.' When Cetus lunged from the water, Perseus drew Medusa into the sun. She opened her eyes. The creature became a mountain of stone before its teeth reached Andromeda's feet, and the broken wave fell around it in silver sheets.

Perseus cut the chains. Andromeda did not look at the head in his hand; she looked at Medusa's snakes, who were arguing over which of them had frightened the monster first. 'Was that you?' Andromeda asked. Perseus began to answer. 'Yes,' Medusa said. Andromeda nodded once, as if a speaking Gorgon were merely the fourth impossible thing she had endured that morning. She wrapped the goatskin around Medusa herself, careful of the fangs. Perseus watched her do it and, for the first time, held the sack as though someone were inside.

They reached Seriphos at night. King Polydectes was feasting with the men who had helped him corner Danaë, Perseus's mother, and drive her to Athena's altar. The hall smelled of lamb fat, spilled wine, and confidence. Polydectes laughed when Perseus entered. 'You promised me the Gorgon's head.' Perseus set the sack on the table. 'I keep my promises.' Medusa heard benches scrape. She heard one servant dive beneath a table and another man whisper a prayer too late. When the goatskin fell away, she opened her eyes only as wide as she chose.

Stone traveled through the hall faster than fire. Polydectes hardened with his cup halfway to his mouth. His friends froze reaching for swords, doors, one another. A musician became marble around a final silent note. Medusa spared the servants, Danaë, the fisherman Dictys, and a dog asleep beside the hearth. The dog woke, inspected the new statues, and lifted its leg against the king. One of Medusa's snakes laughed so hard it bit another.

Athena came for her before sunrise. The goddess took the head from Perseus and fixed it to her aegis with hands that had never trembled. 'Your power will guard cities,' Athena said. Medusa felt the weight of divine armor beneath her and the snakes coiling comfortably around its rim. Far below, Perseus and Andromeda walked toward the harbor. Stheno and Euryale still called across the sea. Athena raised the shield, certain the gaze upon it belonged to her. Medusa closed her eyes. A moment later, when she was ready, she opened them again.

entries.title: Orion
entries.imageAlt: A wet, shadowed archer draws a bow while rising through churning water beneath a pale sky.
entries.teaser: The greatest hunter in the world can walk on water. He cannot outrun the thing beneath it.
story: Orion rose from the Aegean slowly, because a blind man does nothing quickly on black water. The sea reached his waist though the bottom lay a hundred fathoms down; that was Poseidon's blood in him, the old gift that let him walk where ships went. A boy rode on his shoulders, bare heels against Orion's ribs and one soot-black hand tangled in his hair. 'Gull to your left,' Cedalion said. Orion turned toward the wings, raised his bow, and held. He could hear each feather. He could not see the sky. 'East,' the boy reminded him. 'Sun first. Vengeance after.'

On Chios, King Oenopion had promised Orion his daughter Merope if the hunter cleared the island's fields of wild beasts. Orion filled the palace yard with tusks, antlers, hides, and proof. The king delayed the wedding, then delayed it again. Orion answered refusal with wine and went to Merope's chamber after she had barred the door. Oenopion's men seized him before dawn. The king burned out his eyes, dragged him to the shore, and left him among the nets. That night Orion learned what no hunt had taught him: a man could become the beast in a single doorway.

He followed the hammering of the Cyclopes to Lemnos, crawling whenever the ground vanished beneath his feet. Hephaestus found him at the forge entrance, enormous, bleeding, and still trying to threaten anyone who came near. The god of fire did not restore his sight. He set Cedalion, his smallest forge-boy, on Orion's shoulders and told him to walk toward sunrise. So the blind hunter crossed the sea with a child as his eyes. Cedalion named rocks, sails, storms, and once a dolphin that followed them for half a day. Orion began by giving orders. Before they reached the edge of dawn, he had learned to listen.

Helios met them where the morning first touched the water. Sunlight entered Orion's ruined eyes like molten gold. He screamed, fell to his knees without sinking, and opened them upon a world returned: red clouds, green sea, Cedalion's blackened grin. Orion's first clear sight was not Oenopion. It was the boy who had carried him by speaking. His second was Chios on the western horizon. He went back anyway. But Oenopion had hidden in a bronze chamber beneath the earth. Orion broke palace doors and split stone floors until Cedalion said, 'You have your eyes. That does not mean you can see him.' Orion lowered his club and left the island alive.

On Crete he found Artemis running beside a white hind. She knew his name, his crimes, and every boast he had ever made. She also knew he could bring down a charging boar at two hundred paces. The goddess allowed him to hunt beside her under one condition: kill what threatens the balance, never the balance itself. For a season they crossed the mountains as equals. Orion stopped filling courtyards with trophies. He learned the paths mothers used to lead their young to water. When villagers called him the greatest hunter alive, Artemis watched to see whether he would correct them. At first, he did.

Then came the feast at Knossos, the sweet wine, and a room full of men eager to hear a giant praise himself. Orion said there was no creature on earth he could not kill. He said, laughing, that given a year he could empty the whole world of beasts. Deep below the hall, Gaia heard him. The ground opened the next morning and released a scorpion the size of a chariot, black shell shining, tail curved over its back like a second moon. Orion's first arrow shattered. His second glanced away. The scorpion crossed a wheat field without bending a single stalk and came directly for him.

Orion ran toward the coast, not from fear but because Artemis's sacred groves lay inland. The scorpion followed over rock, sand, and the bodies of the hounds that tried to stop it. At the waterline, Orion stepped onto the sea. He waded farther though the waves never climbed above his chest. When the scorpion entered the surf, he dove beneath the foam, circled, and rose behind it with one arrow left. Water streamed from his hair and bowstring. The creature lifted its sting. Orion aimed not at its armor but at the pale joint beneath its tail, the one vulnerable place Artemis had taught him every living thing must have.

He loosed. The arrow struck true. So did the sting. Poison entered Orion's heel and climbed through him colder than the sea. Artemis reached the shore as the scorpion collapsed, its legs carving trenches in the sand. She held Orion upright while the water tried to carry his weight. 'I can ask Zeus to raise you beyond its reach,' she said. Orion remembered Merope behind the barred door, Oenopion beneath the earth, Cedalion patiently naming the world, and every beast he had killed to hear men cheer. 'Do not make me innocent,' he said. 'Make me useful. Let sailors find their road by me. Let hunters see what follows a boast.'

Zeus placed Orion among the winter stars with his belt, his sword, and his bow forever lifted. Gaia raised the scorpion too, but on the opposite side of the sky. When Scorpio climbs, Orion descends; when Orion rises, the scorpion is driven below the horizon. Cedalion grew old steering ships by the bright shoulders of the man he had once guided toward dawn. And every winter, above the same black water, Orion steps out of the eastern sea. He still looks like the greatest hunter in the world. Now, when the last creature turns away unharmed, he knows enough to lower the bow.
